extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of inductive logic, philosophy of science, and scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria for assessing the force, scope, and limits of inductive inferences, derivative/empirical laws, and analogical reasoning; includes guidance on when empirical regularities may be extended in time or place and how to weigh resemblances and differences in analogical arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inferiority of derivative laws to ultimate laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Derivative uniformities (co-existences and sequences between effects) are inferior both in extent and degree of certainty to the ultimate laws from which they are derived.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such derivative uniformities depend on collocations of primeval causes; if collocations vary a totally different set of derivative uniformities may result. Example: the uniform conjunction of day followed by night is derivative on deeper causes (earth's rotation and sun's illumination).

rubrics_metrics.name: Derivative uniformities contingent on collocations
rubrics_metrics.description: Derivative laws are frequently contingent on the particular collocation (combination and arrangement) of causes; changes in collocation can alter or destroy the derivative uniformity even if the ultimate laws remain true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a cause supervenes that counteracts one of the conjoined causes, the derivative effect will not conform to the derived law. Example: if the earth's rotation stopped or a second sun were added, the succession of day and night as observed would no longer obtain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derivative laws more liable to frustration by counteracting causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Because derivative laws arise from combinations of causes, they are liable to frustration from a greater variety of counteracting causes than ultimate laws are.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An ultimate law is frustrated only by counteracting causes that defeat that single cause; a derivative law (combination) can be frustrated by counteraction of any one of the component causes, increasing vulnerability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical/derivative laws admissible only within observed collocations (time/place)
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical or derivative laws are admissible only where the collocations are known by experience to be such as are requisite for the truth of the law; i.e., only within the conditions of time and place confirmed by observation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extending an empirical law beyond observed temporal or spatial limits requires caution; assurances weaken as one projects further from observed cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extension of derivative laws requires knowledge of underlying causes
rubrics_metrics.description: When the causes of a derivative uniformity are known, we can extend the law to adjacent cases in time and place with greater confidence than when only an empirical regularity is known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Knowing causes lets us judge whether known causes may be counteracted and to what spatial extent the causes operate (e.g., reasoning that day/night holds across solar-system bodies because of common causal origin).

rubrics_metrics.name: Probability of future continuation depends on likelihood of destruction or counteraction of causes
rubrics_metrics.description: The chance that a derivative effect (e.g., sunrise tomorrow) will fail depends on the probability that one of its underlying causes will be destroyed or counteracted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess historical stability (e.g., 5,000 years without perceptible counteracting cause) and consider whether any plausible cause exists now that could lead to sudden large effects inconsistent with past regularity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safe temporal extension only to adjacent cases; uncertainty grows with temporal distance
rubrics_metrics.description: Inductive extension of derivative or empirical laws is justifiable only to adjacent cases in time; the farther into the future (or past) one extends, the weaker the induction becomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example contrast: evidence that justifies belief that the sun will rise tomorrow does not equally justify belief that the same will hold twenty thousand years hence because rare combinations or slow accumulations could intervene over longer spans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spatial extension depends on similarity of causal agents and their influence bounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Extending an empirical law to other places requires that the new place is within the influence of the same individual agents (causes); where causes are ascertained, we may extend to the extreme boundaries of their influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the same individual cause is plausibly acting across a region (e.g., planets formed by the same impulse), empirical regularities may be projected across that region; if not, extension is unsafe.

rubrics_metrics.name: When causes are known, one can judge presence of counteracting causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge of the causes behind a phenomenon permits direct assessment of whether any known counteracting causes exist that would defeat the regularity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrasts the bed-ridden savage who hears the cataract (and presumes permanence) with someone who knows the waterfall depends on rock that is wearing away and thus knows the sound may cease in time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogy as resemblance-of-relations can be rigorous if material relation is established
rubrics_metrics.description: Analogy understood as 'resemblance of relations' can, when the fundamentum relationis (the material relation on which consequences depend) is shown, amount to a rigorous induction rather than a weak inference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: describing a mother country and colonies is analogical in relations; if the shared relation (e.g., dependency/management structure) is shown to be the material ground of consequences, the analogy can be as strong as an induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogy as weaker form of induction (resemblance-based inference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Analogy in common usage is reasoning that A and B resemble each other in some respects, a proposition m is true of A, therefore probably true of B — but unlike complete induction, no invariable conjunction between antecedent properties and m has been demonstrated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy fills the gap when the Method of Agreement/Difference cannot be applied; it supplies a probability based on similarity but not certainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shared properties used in analogy must not be known irrelevant to the inferred attribute
rubrics_metrics.description: For an analogical inference to be admissible, the properties in which A and B agree must not be properties known to be unconnected with the attribute m being inferred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If any common properties can be shown by elimination or deduction to be irrelevant to m, the analogical argument is invalidated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resemblance in ultimate vs derivative properties affects force of analogy
rubrics_metrics.description: If the resemblance is in an ultimate property (a causal or fundamental property), resemblance of all derivative properties follows and the analogous inference approaches certainty; resemblance only in derivative properties gives weaker grounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ultimate-property agreement is much stronger because derivative consequences are then more likely to coincide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dissimilarities supply counter-probabilities that must be weighed
rubrics_metrics.description: Every dissimilarity proved between A and B furnishes a counter-probability against the analogical conclusion; known differences may balance or outweigh known resemblances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: lunar resemblances to earth might increase probability of inhabitants, but known differences (no atmosphere, no water) provide strong counter-probabilities that can nullify the analogy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflicting analogies must be compared and weighted
rubrics_metrics.description: When a new case resembles several different reference classes—some of which possess m and some of which do not—these conflicting analogies compete and must be weighed against one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include artifacts that resemble works of multiple schools (Grecian vs Etruscan) or materials (amber with vegetable and mineral properties); weigh the total balance of relevant resemblances and differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strength of analogy proportional to extent of ascertained resemblance versus known difference and unknowns
rubrics_metrics.description: The value of an analogical argument increases with the amount of ascertained resemblance, decreases with ascertained differences, and is undermined by a large unexplored region of unknown properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical heuristic: if B agrees with A in nine of ten known properties, one may assign a rough 9:1 probability to B having the remaining derivative property, but this is only heuristic and depends on the adequacy of known sampling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogy most valuable as heuristic to suggest experiments not as conclusive proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Even weak analogies can be extremely useful in guiding enquiry—suggesting experiments, bringing new facts to light, and proposing discriminating tests (experimenta crucis)—though they do not substitute for complete induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hypotheses inspired by analogy help structure research and prediction; they should be tested rather than accepted uncritically as truths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Belief or instinct is not evidence; evidence requires conformity to fact
rubrics_metrics.description: The universality of causation cannot be established merely by a general human instinct to believe it; belief is not proof—evidence is that which the judging faculty ought to yield to in order to align belief with fact, namely sense and consciousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject appeals to mere habitual belief as justification for claims about external nature; demand evidential support that conforms to observable fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inductive methods presuppose law of universal causation and this presupposition requires justification
rubrics_metrics.description: All inductive methods (Method of Agreement, Method of Difference, etc.) assume that every event has some cause; this assumption (universality of causation) is foundational and must be critically examined rather than taken on authority of instinct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of potential petitio principii: using inductive methods that assume causation to prove causation is circular unless independent warrant for universality is provided.
